study.title: Analgesic Electrical Stimulation Combined with Wrist-Ankle Acupuncture Reduces the Cortical Response to Pain in Patients with Myofasciitis: A Randomized Clinical Trial
study.randomization: The randomization sequence was determined using an online research tool (GraphPad Software), which was unpredictable and eliminated potential experimenter bias. Participants were numbered by the study coordinator in order of recruitment and then randomly assigned to the Experimental Group or the Control Group in a 1:1 ratio.
study.blinding: double-blind; both researchers and participants were blinded
study.population: Male MPS patients recruited from the outpatient clinic of the Rehabilitation Medicine Department at the Shanghai Changhai Hospital
study.inclusion_criteria: male MPS participants between the ages of 18 and 70 years with regional pain, palpable tension striations in localized muscles, fixed pressure points, presence of referred pain, and sensory changes in areas corresponding to myofascia
study.exclusion_criteria: fibromyalgia, a history of neurological problems, adverse reactions to electrical stimulation, and the use of analgesics during the study period

extraction_notes.note: The CONSORT flow diagram (Figure 3) states Excluded (n=3) but lists sub-reasons as 'Adverse reactions to electrical stimulation (n=2)' and 'take painkillers (n=2)', which sum to 4. This inconsistency is in the original paper and cannot be resolved from the text.

No MNI or Talairach coordinates are reported for any brain region. All neuroimaging results are based on fNIRS channel numbers mapped to Brodmann areas via the International 10-20 system, not stereotactic coordinates. Coordinate-based meta-analysis is not possible with this data.
No deqi or sensory sensation questionnaire was used or reported. The pain perception measure was VAS only.
Expectancy, treatment credibility, and blinding success checks were not reported despite the study claiming to be double-blind.
The paper uses both 'DLPFC' and 'DPFC' interchangeably across text and figures to refer to the Dorsolateral Prefrontal Cortex. These appear to refer to the same region.

The exact blinding procedure is unclear. The paper states 'both researchers and participants were blinded' but does not detail how blinding was achieved for the experimental group receiving active electrical stimulation versus the control group resting.

No absolute beta values are provided in tables for the ROI comparisons. Results for FPA (P < .01) and DLPFC (P < 0.001) are only given as statistical significance levels. Exact beta values are shown only in Figure 7 which is a bar graph without numeric values listed in text.

Cortical activation maps (Figure 4), channel correlation heatmaps (Figure 5), ROI correlation heatmaps (Figure 6), and regression coefficient bar charts (Figure 7) are presented as figures without accompanying numeric tables. Exact numeric values for most neural results are not available from the text alone.

Table 3 labels are 'VASbefore' and 'VASafter' which are interpreted as pre- and post-intervention/rest VAS values. However, the paper does not clarify whether VAS was measured during pain stimulation or between stimulation sessions.

The paper states the study design is 'double-blind' but only one active treatment (WAA-TENS) and one rest condition are compared. There is no sham stimulation arm, which limits interpretation of blinding and placebo control.
No follow-up timepoint was assessed. The study is a single-session experiment with pre/post measurements only.
Only male participants were enrolled. The authors acknowledge this as a limitation and that results may not generalize to women.
The paper uses 'DPFC' in Figure 6 captions but 'DLPFC' in the body text and Figure 7 caption. Both appear to refer to Dorsolateral Prefrontal Cortex (BA 9, 46).

The flow chart (Figure 3) exclusion reasons list sums to 4 participants (n=2 adverse reactions + n=2 painkillers) but states n=3 excluded. This may be an OCR error or a typographic error in the original paper.
